Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 2 detected *p* values.

table.formatted: If remove_nonsignificant=TRUE is set, ResIN() forces to zero all edge-weights whose p-values exceed the default threshold of p < 0.05; this threshold can be altered with the sign_threshold argument.
table.expanded: If remove_nonsignificant=TRUE is set, ResIN() forces to zero all edge-weights whose p-values exceed the default threshold of p < 0.05; this threshold can be altered with the sign_threshold argument.

table.formatted: Relative to a fixed per-edge threshold (e.g., p < 0.05), this approach adapts the rejection boundary to the global distribution of p-values and controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among retained edges, typically yielding greater power while maintaining a principled error rate <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Benjamini & Yekutieli, 2001)</ref>.
table.expanded: Relative to a fixed per-edge threshold (e.g., p < 0.05), this approach adapts the rejection boundary to the global distribution of p-values and controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among retained edges, typically yielding greater power while maintaining a principled error rate (Benjamini & Yekutieli, 2001).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "Relative to a fixed per-edge threshold (e.g., p < 0.05), this approach adapts the rejection boundary to the global distribution of p-values and controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among retained edges, typically yielding greater power while maintaining a principled error rate (Benjamini & Yekutieli, 2001)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 23 columns across 3 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Introducing ResIN: An Applied Tutorial to the Response-Item-Networks Package for R

author.affiliation:

text.text: This tutorial introduces ResIN, a package for the R programming language designed to estimate, visualize, and analyze Response-Item Networks (ResIN ).
ResIN is an increasingly popular method for exploring complex attitude systems as sparse, spatially interpretable networks.

The package simplifies and unifies the underlying workflow while offering a range of convenience features, including network plotting, community detection, individual-level score extraction, bootstrap-based uncertainty estimation, and the export of ResIN objects to other statistical software environments.

Using political attitudes as an example, we provide an overview of the ResIN method, its computational implementation in R, and demonstrate the utility of key package features through an applied replication tutorial based on a recent study by Lüders et al., 2024.
The paper concludes by briefly situating the ResIN method and package among several conceptually and methodologically related belief network models currently available in R.

The study of complex socio-political attitude systems is currently booming across the social and behavioral sciences (e.g., Bakker & Lelkes, 2022; Baldassarri & Goldberg, 2014; Bertero et al., 2024; Boutyline, 2017; Boutyline & Vaisey, 2017; Brandt, 2022; Brandt et al., 2019; DellaPosta, 2020; Fishman & Davis, 2022; Van Noord et al., 2025; Zwicker et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The study of complex socio-political attitude systems is currently booming across the social and behavioral sciences (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bakker & Lelkes, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Baldassarri & Goldberg, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bertero et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Boutyline, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Boutyline & Vaisey, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Brandt, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Brandt et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">DellaPosta, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Fishman & Davis, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Van Noord et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Zwicker et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Arguably, statistical belief network models (BNMs) capture the inherent complexity of such systems more faithfully than many conventional latent scaling and dimensionality reduction techniques (Brandt & Sleegers, 2021; Dalege et al., 2016; Quayle, 2025; Warncke, 2025), allowing researchers to explore macro-and component-level properties in much richer detail whilst avoiding taxing and often unrealistic assumptions that conventional statistics impose on such systems (e.g., Chen et al., 2025; Quayle, 2025; Warncke et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Arguably, statistical belief network models (BNMs) capture the inherent complexity of such systems more faithfully than many conventional latent scaling and dimensionality reduction techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brandt & Sleegers, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Dalege et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Quayle, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Warncke, 2025)</ref>, allowing researchers to explore macro-and component-level properties in much richer detail whilst avoiding taxing and often unrealistic assumptions that conventional statistics impose on such systems (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Quayle, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Warncke et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Response-Item Networks (ResIN ) constitute a novel class of BNM that combines statistical network modeling with the spatial interpretability of established dimensionality-reduction methods (Carpentras et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Response-Item Networks (ResIN ) constitute a novel class of BNM that combines statistical network modeling with the spatial interpretability of established dimensionality-reduction methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carpentras et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In a nutshell, ResIN locates each possible response option across survey items (e.g., strongly agree, somewhat agree, neutral, somewhat disagree, strongly disagree) within a theoretically interpretable latent space.
When a given pair of attitudes is frequently co-endorsed, such as anti-abortion and anti-gun-control positions among the US electorate, ResIN maps them closely together.
By contrast, attitude pairings that are rarely co-endorsed, such as anti-abortion and pro-gun-control positions, appear farther apart in ResIN -space.
By simultaneously modeling patterns of relative attraction and repulsion across all possible choice pairings, ResIN recovers the principal axes of agreement and division within attitude networks.
Furthermore, ResIN provides a more granular angle of investigation than extant BNMs because it generates belief networks at the item-response level.
1 The method can thus uncover complex interactions between-and asymmetries among-attitude clusters associated with supporters of different political parties, social groups, or strata.

Several recent studies demonstrate the potential of this approach, including on vaccination uptake (Carpentras et al., 2022), ideological cue taking (Lüders et al., 2024), and comparative belief systems structure (Chen et al., 2025; Warncke et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Several recent studies demonstrate the potential of this approach, including on vaccination uptake <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Carpentras et al., 2022)</ref>, ideological cue taking <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Lüders et al., 2024)</ref>, and comparative belief systems structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Chen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Warncke et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: 1 In the context of quantitative survey research, issue items typically refer to close-ended questions probing for respondents' positions on particular issues, such as the minimum wage, abortion, and CO2 emissions.
Item responses denote endorsed answer choices to such questions.
For instance, "strongly opposing cuts to the minimum wage", "favoring restrictions to abortion" or "being neutral on carbon tax emissions" are examples of item responses to the above listed items.

This paper introduces ResIN, a new software package for estimating, visualizing, and interpreting ResIN graphs in R. In Section 2, we begin with a theoretical and mathematical overview of the ResIN method.
This is followed by a discussion of the R-package design philosophy in Section 3.1.
Next, we demonstrate how to install and test the package and illustrate the basic utility and output of the flagship ResIN() function in Section 3.2.

A more comprehensive workflow tutorial in Section 3.3 replicates the main findings of a recent study by Lüders et al., 2024. This tutorial covers the use of node-level covariates-that is, core demographic and psychological characteristics of respondents who endorse particular issue positions (Section 3.3.1)-as well as individual-level position scores along the dominant axis of ResIN graphs (Section 3.3.2) and the use of the ResIN bootstrap functions to quantify statistical uncertainty around network estimates (Section 3.3.3).
text.formatted: A more comprehensive workflow tutorial in Section 3.3 replicates the main findings of a recent study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lüders et al., 2024.</ref> This tutorial covers the use of node-level covariates-that is, core demographic and psychological characteristics of respondents who endorse particular issue positions (Section 3.3.1)-as well as individual-level position scores along the dominant axis of ResIN graphs (Section 3.3.2) and the use of the ResIN bootstrap functions to quantify statistical uncertainty around network estimates (Section 3.3.3).

text.text: We cover more advanced capabilities of the package in the remainder of the applied tutorial component of this manuscript.

These include edge, node-, and graph-level descriptive statistics (Section 3.4), network cluster detection (Section 3.5), network pruning (Section 3.6), modeling multimodal ResIN -networks (Section 3.7), and exporting ResIN-objects to other statistical environments within R, Python, Julia, and Gephi (Section 3.8).

In Section 4, we briefly situate ResIN within a rapidly expanding family of statistical belief network models, hoping to provide readers with elementary guidance about the method's overall scope, its relative strengths, and its shortcomings compared to other conceptually and computationally related alternatives available in R. Final Section 5 discusses some important limitations users should be aware of when working with ResIN, while offering practical advice and ideas about future conceptual advances in the method.
ResIN provides a model of co-endorsement patterns contained within positional attitude systems (Carpentras et al., 2024).
text.formatted: ResIN provides a model of co-endorsement patterns contained within positional attitude systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carpentras et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Broadly understood, positional attitudes denote valenced sentiments towards socially or politically relevant issues.
For instance, opposing cuts to the minimum wage, being neutral on carbon taxes, or supporting equal pay for women and men constitute positional attitudes (e.g., Hatemi & McDermott, 2016).
text.formatted: For instance, opposing cuts to the minimum wage, being neutral on carbon taxes, or supporting equal pay for women and men constitute positional attitudes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hatemi & McDermott, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: If such attitudes are socially shared, they develop links within collective belief-systems and thus serve as definable and recognizable attributes both of groupness and social selfhood (O'Reilly et al., 2024; Quayle, 2025).
text.formatted: If such attitudes are socially shared, they develop links within collective belief-systems and thus serve as definable and recognizable attributes both of groupness and social selfhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(O'Reilly et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Quayle, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: ResIN presumes that the more a given pair of attitudes (e.g., simultaneously supporting equal pay for men and women while opposing cuts to the minimum wage) is socially co-endorsed, the more closely this pair is located within a latent attitude space (Carpentras et al., 2024).
text.formatted: ResIN presumes that the more a given pair of attitudes (e.g., simultaneously supporting equal pay for men and women while opposing cuts to the minimum wage) is socially co-endorsed, the more closely this pair is located within a latent attitude space <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carpentras et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Spatial proximity between any node pair in ResIN can be interpreted as abstract (or ideological) distance between those item-responses, or equivalently, as social distance between respondents within the latent space (Quayle, 2025).
text.formatted: Spatial proximity between any node pair in ResIN can be interpreted as abstract (or ideological) distance between those item-responses, or equivalently, as social distance between respondents within the latent space <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Quayle, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: ResIN models all possible pairwise interactions among a given set of attitudes within a single statistical network.
In ResIN -networks, attitude responses form the nodes while the edges determine the associative strength between them.
The method assumes that only sufficiently co-endorsed (i.e., positively correlated) node pairs attract one another.
At the same time, all attitude nodes experience a constant repulsive force.

The core of the ResIN method involves a computational simulation that balances these opposing forces, relying on a force-directed network plotting algorithm (Fruchterman & Reingold, 1991), which yields a spatially interpretable, theoretically meaningful latent structure in which both attitudes and people can be co-located (Carpentras et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The core of the ResIN method involves a computational simulation that balances these opposing forces, relying on a force-directed network plotting algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Fruchterman & Reingold, 1991)</ref>, which yields a spatially interpretable, theoretically meaningful latent structure in which both attitudes and people can be co-located <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carpentras et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We next describe the main computational steps involved in ResIN ; more comprehensive and applied introductions to the method itself, including detailed theoretical and practical reasons behind each step, can be found in Carpentras et al., 2024 and Warncke et al., 2026.
text.formatted: We next describe the main computational steps involved in ResIN ; more comprehensive and applied introductions to the method itself, including detailed theoretical and practical reasons behind each step, can be found in <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Carpentras et al., 2024 and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Warncke et al., 2026.</ref>

text.text: The first step in ResIN involves transforming an n × K data table, X, where n equals the number of respondents and K the number of available (survey) items.
Throughout, we index respondents by p ∈ {1, . . . , n}, survey items by k ∈ {1, . . . , K}, and the response options belonging to a given item by r.
Each cell (p, k) of X thus contains the response provided by respondent p to item k, which we denote X [p, k].
text.formatted: Each cell (p, k) of X thus contains the response provided by respondent p to item k, which we denote X <ref type="bibr">[p, k]</ref>.

text.text: From X, a new table, Y, is obtained by expanding every response level contained in X into a separate column of binary data (a process also known as dummy-and one-hot-coding).
Each new column within the expanded data frame is set to 1 if a given response was endorsed, and 0 otherwise.
More specifically, let R k = {R k,1 , . . . , R k,J k } denote the set of response options available for item k, where J k = |R k | and R k,r is the r-th such option, with1 ≤ r ≤ J k .
For each item k, ResIN produces J k new columns, d k,1 , . . . , d k,J k , so that every column of Y is uniquely identified by the item-response pair (k, r).
text.formatted: For each item k, ResIN produces J k new columns, d k,1 , . . . , d k,J k , so that every column of Y is uniquely identified by the item-response pair <ref type="bibr">(k, r)</ref>.

text.text: The entry of column d k,r for respondent p can then be written as:
Table Y is therefore of dimension n × s, with s = K k=1 J k .
Expression (2) provides an example thereof.
Next, a sparse, s × s pairwise-correlation table Z is obtained from Y by correlating every pair of dummy-coded columns that stem from different original items.
Writing the second item-response pair as (l, m), the entry of Z corresponding to columns d k,r and d l,m is
By default, ResIN relies on the Pearson correlation but the method also works with tetrachoric correlations (both approaches are implemented in the ResIN package).
2 An example is provided in the following expression (4).
2 The basic choice between Pearson and tetrachoric correlations is governed by a closely related consideration.

For two binary indicators the Pearson correlation reduces to the ϕ coefficient, whose attainable maximum is a function of the marginal endorsement rates: for options endorsed by proportions π1 ≤ π2, ϕ cannot exceed π1(1 -π2)/[π2(1 -π1)], which falls well below unity whenever the two marginals are dissimilar.
Two strongly associated positions endorsed by 10 and 50 per cent of the sample, respectively, can attain a ϕ of at most 0.33.

Since ResIN edge weights determine attraction strength in the layout, this attenuation is not always innocuous as it systematically shrinks the edges of unpopular response options and thereby displaces them toward the periphery of the latent space.

Tetrachoric correlations remove the dependence on marginals by positing a bivariate normal latent continuum underlying each pair of dichotomies, and are advisable whenever endorsement rates vary substantially across the response set-the typical situation with skewed or strongly polarized items.
However, this correction does not come for free: tetrachorics carry larger standard errors than ϕ, and they can become unstable or undefined when a cell of the 2 × 2 table is empty or near-empty.
Finally, the algorithm obtains the positive, undirected, weighted adjacency matrix Z ′ by clipping all negative entries in Z to zero.

This step is necessary as negative edges cannot be processed by conventional force-directed network plotting algorithms. Carpentras et al., 2024 have shown that setting correlation pairs to zero results in no noticeable loss in precision in the estimation of node locations in a structured latent space.
text.formatted: This step is necessary as negative edges cannot be processed by conventional force-directed network plotting algorithms. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Carpentras et al., 2024</ref> have shown that setting correlation pairs to zero results in no noticeable loss in precision in the estimation of node locations in a structured latent space.

text.text: Equation ( 5) gives the general rule, where Z ab denotes the entry in row a and column b of Z under any fixed ordering a, b ∈ {1, . . . , s} of the dummy columns, while Equation ( 6) performs the thresholding on an example.
text.formatted: Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_5">5</ref>) gives the general rule, where Z ab denotes the entry in row a and column b of Z under any fixed ordering a, b ∈ {1, . . . , s} of the dummy columns, while Equation ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_6">6</ref>) performs the thresholding on an example.

text.text: After obtaining the positive entry-only correlation matrix, a force-directed network layout algorithm is applied to determine the two-dimensional position of each response node.
By default, ResIN relies on the algorithm of Fruchterman and Reingold (1991), which treats nodes as negatively charged particles connected by Hooke-like springs.
text.formatted: By default, ResIN relies on the algorithm of <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Fruchterman and Reingold (1991)</ref>, which treats nodes as negatively charged particles connected by Hooke-like springs.

text.text: While all nodes repel each other, the edges retained in Z ′ pull connected nodes back together with a strength proportional to the correlation weight.
Consequently, strongly correlated response nodes appear closer together while tenuously (and un-)connected pairs drift further apart.
(Appendix Equations ( 9)-( 14) provide full details on the Fruchterman and Reingold (1991) algorithm as implemented in ResIN.)
text.formatted: (Appendix Equations ( <ref type="formula">9</ref>)-( <ref type="formula">14</ref>) provide full details on the <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Fruchterman and Reingold (1991)</ref> algorithm as implemented in ResIN.)

text.text: Thus, Z ′ is mapped onto a 2 × s coordinate matrix, C, providing the (x, y) coordinates of each item-response node once the force-directed layout algorithm has converged.
We illustrate this step with hypothetical coordinate values in Equation ( 7):

text.text: The final step in ResIN involves a principal components (PC) rotation of the node coordinate matrix, which ensures the spatial interpretability of the dominant latent dimension of a particular attitude system.
We mathematically describe this procedure in Appendix A.2.
In a nutshell, the PC rotation preserves all pairwise distances while removing the arbitrary rotation obtained from the force-directed network plotting algorithm.
This results in a more interpretable embedding whose x-and y-axes correspond to the first and second principal components of shared variance among the attitude node locations.

Expression (8) illustrates that variance along the 3 We emphasize that the restriction to two dimensions is a visualization and interpretability choice in the current computational implementation of the ResIN method rather than the outcome of a formal dimensionality criterion.

ResIN embeds response nodes in the plane because a two-dimensional layout can be read directly off the page and because the dominant axis is ordinarily the quantity of substantive interest; the underlying force-directed algorithm generalizes to higher dimensions, although the present implementation returns a twodimensional layout by default.
No formal criterion establishes that two dimensions are optimal for visualizing or spatially situating a given attitude system.

However, one practical benefit of the PC rotation is that the axes are ordered by the variance they capture, so users can gauge how much of the layout's structure is carried by the second dimension relative to the first.
Researchers for whom the dimensionality of an attitude system is itself the object of inquiry should address that question with a method designed for it, such as EGA (Section 4).
The rotated coordinate matrix C ′ provides the two-dimensional position of every response node and thereby defines the spatial embedding of the ResIN graph.

More specifically, each column of C ′ corresponds to one response option d k,r and becomes a node in the plotted network, while the non-zero entries of the weighted adjacency matrix Z ′ determine which pairs of nodes are connected by edges and how strongly they attract one another in the visualization.
Thus, C ′ supplies the node coordinates, whereas Z ′ supplies the edge structure and edge weights.

In practice, the resulting graph can be visualized by placing each response node d k,r at its rotated coordinates (x k,r , y k,r ) and drawing weighted, undirected edges between all pairs of nodes for which Z ′ ab > 0.
text.formatted: In practice, the resulting graph can be visualized by placing each response node d k,r at its rotated coordinates (x k,r , y k,r ) and drawing weighted, undirected edges between all pairs of nodes for which Z ′ ab > 0.

text.text: The resulting network representation preserves the spatial logic recovered by the force-directed layout and subsequent principal-components rotation: response options that are frequently co-endorsed tend to appear close together, whereas more weakly associated or unconnected responses appear farther apart.

Columns of C ′ become response nodes d k,r positioned at (x k,r , y k,r ), while non-zero entries in Z ′ determine the weighted edges between them.
Once plotted, ResIN graphs can be inspected both visually and statistically for substantive structure.

Informative features typically include the emergence of clusters or communities of mutually compatible attitudes, asymmetries in the spatial arrangement of issue positions, and differences in node centrality that may indicate especially influential or representative response options within the broader attitude system.
We return to descriptive and inferential tools for each of these aspects in greater detail below.
Following a "simple by default, flexible when needed" approach, the ResIN package was crafted around ResIN::ResIN() as a single, flagship utility function.

Since ResIN's core user base largely consists of social scientists with limited to intermediate statistical programming skills, we wrote ResIN() to work 'out-of-the-box' for the most common belief network research and analysis tasks.
To be fully operable, ResIN() thus solely requires a user-supplied survey dataset via the df argument.

At the same time, the function exposes a high degree of argument-based configurability, allowing users to tailor correlation estimation, missing-data handling, pruning decisions, plotting behavior, and downstream network-analytic steps to their specific needs.

To facilitate transparent and iterative workflows, ResIN() also stores important, intermediate products of the estimation pipeline covered across Equations ( 4), (7), and (8) (e.g., the dummy-coded response matrix, network adjacency matrix, cluster assignment quantities, and additional auxiliary objects), enabling more advanced users to inspect intermediate results, extract particular components for further analyses, and refine their modeling choices as needed.
text.formatted: To facilitate transparent and iterative workflows, ResIN() also stores important, intermediate products of the estimation pipeline covered across Equations ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_3">4</ref>), (7), and (8) (e.g., the dummy-coded response matrix, network adjacency matrix, cluster assignment quantities, and additional auxiliary objects), enabling more advanced users to inspect intermediate results, extract particular components for further analyses, and refine their modeling choices as needed.

text.text: Beyond implementing the ResIN -method, the ResIN() function thus unifies several routine belief network analysis tasks under a single software umbrella.

The function particularly streamlines network plotting workflows by automating data reprocessing and supplying several sensible default parameters to ggplot2 as primary plotting engine (Wickham et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The function particularly streamlines network plotting workflows by automating data reprocessing and supplying several sensible default parameters to ggplot2 as primary plotting engine <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Wickham et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Besides calculating various network, node, and edge-level statistics, ResIN() can also perform basic statistical inference tasks about node-level co-variates, detect network clusters, and estimate psychometric-type scores for survey respondents based on attitude node locations within the ResIN layout.
These capabilities can be activated by user-defined arguments which will be covered in more detail from Section 3.3 onward.
The principles of interoperability and replicability further guided the package design.

By default, ResIN() returns a self-contained, classed object that stores core results (edge-and node tables, adjacency matrix, plots, and auxiliary objects) alongside reproducibility metadata (e.g., package version, call, and input identifiers).
Moreover, the package ships with explicit coercion and export methods that allow users to port ResIN-objects to other, commonly used graph ecosystems without manual reformatting.

In particular, the as.igraph() and as.qgraph() methods enable immediate integration with the igraph (Csardi & Nepusz, 2006) and qgraph (Epskamp et al., 2012) toolchains, while as.network() supports workflows in the statnet ecosystem (Handcock et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In particular, the as.igraph() and as.qgraph() methods enable immediate integration with the igraph <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Csardi & Nepusz, 2006)</ref> and qgraph <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Epskamp et al., 2012)</ref> toolchains, while as.network() supports workflows in the statnet ecosystem <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Handcock et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, lightweight cross-language exporters facilitate reproducible downstream analysis beyond R: as.networkx() and as.graphsjl() generate edge-and node tables that can seamlessly be re-imported into NetworkX in Python and Graphs.jl in Julia, while as.gephi() writes Gephi-readable edge-(and optional node-) tables for external visualization and inspection (Hogervorst, 2022).
text.formatted: Finally, lightweight cross-language exporters facilitate reproducible downstream analysis beyond R: as.networkx() and as.graphsjl() generate edge-and node tables that can seamlessly be re-imported into NetworkX in Python and Graphs.jl in Julia, while as.gephi() writes Gephi-readable edge-(and optional node-) tables for external visualization and inspection <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hogervorst, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these methods preserves all node-and edge-level attributes obtained with ResIN as tabular metadata.
The task of deriving uncertainty estimates for network quantities can easily lead to computational and programming bottlenecks.
This is why ResIN ships with three sequential helper functions which are designed to simplify the input, execution, and results extraction tasks by compartmentalizing each step.
First, the ResIN_boots_prepare() function specifies which network object(s) and properties users wish to resample.
Next, ResIN_boots_execute() handles repeated network estimation while providing optional back-end utilities for CPU-parallelism.
Finally, ResIN_boots_ extract() provides a forward-search and concatenate utility, helping users to extract and obtain statistical summaries from their target quantities of interest.
We cover the basic usage of the ResIN-bootstrap functions in Section 3.3.3.

In Appendix A.3, we provide more detail on the computational implementation of the ResIN() function and the packaged bootstrapping utilities, including other R packages ResIN depends on.

In this section, we illustrate the basic usage of the ResIN package with a complete workflow tutorial, covering basic data cleaning and pre-processing, network estimation, interpretation, and statistical inference tasks typically involved in ResIN analyses.

Our example is based on a replication of Lüders et al., 2024-'Attitude networks as intergroup realities: Using network-modeling to research attitude-identity relationships in polarized political contexts'. Lüders et al., 2024 use ResIN to investigate whether co-endorsement patterns among political attitudes reveal meaningful attitude-identity relationships using the United States of America as a case study of mass political polarization.
text.formatted: Our example is based on a replication of <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lüders et al., 2024-'</ref>Attitude networks as intergroup realities: Using network-modeling to research attitude-identity relationships in polarized political contexts'. <ref type="bibr">Lüders et al., 2024 use</ref> ResIN to investigate whether co-endorsement patterns among political attitudes reveal meaningful attitude-identity relationships using the United States of America as a case study of mass political polarization.

text.text: The central expectation is that the latent structure of political attitudes should align with partisan identities and thereby reveal which issues are perceived to "belong" to opposing political camps.

The authors find that the estimated attitude network recovers two conflictive partisan belief systems; the spatial location of response nodes carries substantial information about latent partisan identity.

Both findings imply that attitude networks can be used not only to summarize opinion structure, but also to study how attitudes function as socially meaningful cues in intergroup perception and identity management.

The original authors agreed to publish their primary data-set as part of ResIN-package version 2.0.0+ as a dedicated data object that is accessible via ResIN::BrJSocPsychol_2024 or by calling data(BrJSocPsychol_2024).
The dataset consists of eight, Likert-type political attitude questions fielded to a nationally diverse sample of 402 US adults in 2020.
The attitudes cover positions on the legality of abortion, income inequality, illegal migration, welfare spending, gay marriage, environmental protection, gun control, and aid to African Americans.

We commence by loading the original data and selecting the same attitude variables as Lüders et al., 2024. We further apply more informative variable and response option labels with tidyverse functions (Wickham et al., 2019).

text.text: Here, we simply infer the meaning of the different political attitudes as either left-leaning or right-leaning, assuming for example that left-wingers usually endorse abortion rights while rightwingers oppose these.
We will describe a more rigorous empirical approach based on co-variates later on.
For now, it suffices to conclude that the right-wing attitude space appears more mixed as it incorporates both neutral and even some of the moderate-left leaning response options.
In this section, we hone in on the spatial embeddings within ResIN networks.

Because ResIN arranges response nodes along the axes of greatest co-endorsement variance, the spatial location of attitude nodes can be read as an empirical ordering of positions along a dominant latent division.

As discussed in Section 5, this ordering is a descriptive summary of co-endorsement structure rather than an estimate of a latent variable in the measurement-theoretic sense, and its substantive interpretation should therefore be externally validated.
We offer one such approach in the remainder of this section.
The node location on the main spatial axis can be accessed via ResIN_out$ResIN_nodeframe$ x.

To make the above hypotheses testable, we add respondents' own partisan self-identification (partisan) and their dislike of the Democratic party relative to their dislike of the Republican party (dem_bias) to the working dataset in the code snippet below.
To ease interpretation, we recoded partisan attachments to fall within the unit interval, with democratic affiliation coded as 0 (more blue), Independents as 0.5, and Republicans at 1 (more red).

To differentiate our co-variates from the actual issue position attitudes we wish to make inferences about, we can simply supply character vectors to the node_vars and node_covars arguments of the ResIN() function.
Furthermore, since we would like to have access to the means of our two co-variates at the response node level, we need to specify node_costats=c("mean","mean").
This argument tells ResIN to obtain the node-level mean from each co-variate (hence the double call of "mean").
Other node_costats possibilities include the median (node_costats="median"), standard deviation ("sd"), or variance ("var").

To further enhance the visual output, we select the red-blue color palette (color_palette="RdBu") and reverse the direction with direction=-1 to ensure that item nodes endorsed by more Democrats appear in blue and Republicans in red.

The stored ResIN_out$ResIN_nodeframe object contains both node-level co-statistics, i.e., the average partisan endorsement (partisan_mean) and the affective bias against the Democratic party (dem_bias_mean) as attested to by our summary() calls below.
In resulting Figure 5, we opted to visualize the former co-statistic with the aid of the plot_whichstat= "partisan_mean" argument.

text.text: We have just shown that there is a strong statistical relationship between response nodes and average partisanship per node.
Yet, what about survey respondents themselves?
How strong is this association at the level of respondents?
ResIN() is capable of obtaining scores for all survey-takers by averaging the node positions among the attitude nodes that a given individual endorsed.
These scores are stored in an n × 2 data-frame called ResIN_out$ResIN_scores; the major axis scores appear as raw_x and the minor axis component as raw_y.
ResIN() also obtains two further types of score estimates which are based on partial pooling of item and individual level means.
First, the package implements a simple heuristic approach, heur_x, which weighs node-level means by their relative popularity.
Second, a more principled strategy centered around empirical Bayesian shrinkage (Efron & Morris, 1973) imposes a datadriven penalty on both sparsely populated and overly extreme estimates (eb_x).
text.formatted: Second, a more principled strategy centered around empirical Bayesian shrinkage <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Efron & Morris, 1973)</ref> imposes a datadriven penalty on both sparsely populated and overly extreme estimates (eb_x).

text.text: We recommend either of these options if users experience large discrepancies in item response popularity or if there is substantial missingness among the individual-level data.
For the sake of illustration, we correlate the empirical-Bayes scores with individual-level partisan bias below.
The probability values adjusted for multiple tests are in the p.adj object.

[1] 0 Although somewhat smaller in magnitude, the above code output suggests that ResIN is capable of recovering a considerable association (r ≈ 0.7) between participants' ResIN -derived latent space scores and their partisan-affective bias.
Above, we have shown that ResIN -derived attitude-node locations are strongly associated with respondents' average partisan identities.
But what about statistical uncertainty?

How can we be sure that this finding is robust to both sampling and other sources of error, particularly with respect to the additional uncertainty introduced by ResIN 's stochastic force-directed algorithm?

Based on our running example, we showcase a simple workflow example for how to initiate, execute, and visualize bootstrapped uncertainty estimates around the above-obtained correlation coefficient between x-axis node location and political partisanship.
Appendix A.3.2 covers a more thorough exposition of the ResIN bootstrapping verbs and their arguments.

In brief, we first use the ResIN_boots_prepare() function to declare the ResIN-object we'd like to bootstrap and to determine the basic kind of bootstrapping procedure (i.e., boots_type="resample" to draw uncertainty bounds around parameters of interest, or boots_type="permute" to generate permutation-test null-hypothesis distributions).
Second, we use the ResIN_boots_execute() function to carry out the planned bootstrapping procedure (optionally leveraging CPU parallelism with parallel=TRUE).
Third and finally, the ResIN_boots_extract() function can be used to extract, concatenate, and optionally provide statistical summaries of the desired, resampled parameters.

Sticking with the analyses of the previous section, we will use the bootstrapping function to re-estimate the same ResIN -network with the mean-level of respondents' partisan identities as node-level co-variate of interest.
To this end, we first re-specify a more bare-bones call to ResIN() which features only the arguments we need for this specific task, i.e., node_covars=c("partisan") and node_costats=c("mean").
Importantly, we disable any superfluous feature: network_ stats=FALSE,generate_ggplot=FALSE,plot_ggplot=FALSE,ResIN_scores=FALSE,detect_ clusters=FALSE.

We recommend disabling all unnecessary arguments as best practice in bootstrapping workloads, especially for larger networks and bootstrap loads (i.e., 1,000 and above iterations on most consumer-based computer hardware), as this will significantly reduce computational demand and estimation times.
Finally, please note that we kept the anchoring node (left_anchor="legal_abort_++") unchanged.
As covered in Section 3.3.1, ResIN does not possess any pre-configured understanding of the substantive 'meaning' of resulting spatial layouts.

Recall that due to the PCA-rotation of the resulting force-directed layout, ResIN -solutions can be randomly mirrored such that all ideologically right-leaning attitudes might appear on the left-hand side while all left-leaning attitudes might appear on the right-hand side of the resulting layout.

6 Defining a single, directional anchoring node that is highly indicative of the substantive meaning of the underlying latent (ideological) space therefore ensures consistency in the overall spatial orientation (and hence, substantive interpretation) across ResIN() runs.

7   ResIN_barebones <-ResIN(Items_plus_Covs, node_vars = c("legal_abort", "equalize_incomes", "keep_immigrants", "welfare_spending", "gay_marriage", "protect_environ", "gun_control", "aid_blacks"), node_covars = c("partisan"), node_costats = c("mean"), left_anchor = "legal_abort_++", network_stats = FALSE, generate_ggplot = FALSE, plot_ggplot = FALSE, ResIN_scores = FALSE, detect_clusters = FALSE) At this stage, we're ready to move to implementing the actual bootstrapping procedure.
text.formatted: 7   ResIN_barebones <-ResIN(Items_plus_Covs, node_vars = c("legal_abort", "equalize_incomes", "keep_immigrants", "welfare_spending", "gay_marriage", "protect_environ", "gun_control", "aid_blacks"), node_covars = c("partisan"), node_costats = c("mean"), left_anchor = "legal_abort_++", network_stats = FALSE, generate_ggplot = FALSE, plot_ggplot = FALSE, ResIN_scores = FALSE, detect_clusters = FALSE) At this stage, we're ready to move to implementing the actual bootstrapping procedure.

text.text: Since we ultimately want to generate uncertainty estimates around the correlation coefficient of interest (r x;party = 0.87), we should specify boots_type="resample" inside the ResIN_boots_ prepare() function.
We further set the parallel argument to TRUE and allocate all available cores to the task at hand with detect_cores=TRUE to take full advantage of parallelism inside ResIN_boots_execute().

We further set the seed_boots argument to ensure replicability of the entire bootstrapping procedure (and not just singular runs of ResIN() within each bootstrap iteration which are set with the regular seed argument).
8 6 ResIN() simply reverses the spatial mirror-effect for all 'mirrored' solutions if left_anchor is set.
This check is performed independently within each bootstrap iteration, so that every resampled layout is brought into a common orientation before node positions are extracted and aggregated.

Thus, setting the left_anchor argument is especially important for bootstrapping ResIN networks as random flips in the spatial orientation of the dominant axis could contaminate inferences based on the (average) spatial location of nodes -as in our present example.
7 This safeguard is only as reliable as the directional anchor itself.

Because the correction is applied conditional on the estimated position of a single node, sampling error in that node's location does not remain local but propagates to the entire layout as a discrete, network-wide reflection.

The relevant quantity is the anchor's expected distance from the layout centroid relative to its own resampling variability: the share of mis-oriented iterations is approximately Φ(-|µa|/σa), where Φ(•) denotes the standard normal distribution function and µa and σa denote the mean and standard deviation of the anchor's bootstrapped x-coordinate.
This is why we do not recommend very sparsely endorsed response nodes as anchor candidates.

As they enter the association matrix with imprecisely estimated correlations, they may forfeit most of their surviving edges once within-item and negative correlations are removed (Equation 5); weakly connected nodes are positioned near-arbitrarily by the Fruchterman-Reingold algorithm.
text.formatted: As they enter the association matrix with imprecisely estimated correlations, they may forfeit most of their surviving edges once within-item and negative correlations are removed (Equation <ref type="formula" target="#formula_5">5</ref>); weakly connected nodes are positioned near-arbitrarily by the Fruchterman-Reingold algorithm.

text.text: As a rule of thumb, we therefore recommend anchoring on a node endorsed by at least 5% of the sample -a criterion our own anchor comfortably satisfies -and confirming that it occupies a clearly lateral position in the full-sample solution.

text.text: The extract function performs a forward search operation across all resampled networks, retrieving each object (typically vectors or scalars stored inside each ResINoutput list) exactly matching a particular search term.
Thus, ResIN_boots_extract() typically returns a numbered list of the same length as the number of pre-specified bootstrap iterations.

In our example, we first search the bootstrapped output list for what="x" to retrieve all xaxis node positions across all resampled networks (which the function compiles from all nested ResIN_out$ResIN_nodeframe$x vectors).

In other words, ResIN_boots_extract(ResIN_ executed,what="x") searches our large bootstrap results list (ResIN_executed) for all instances of the x-axis coordinate locations (i.e., the content of each ResIN_out$ResIN_nodeframe$ x vector) which we conveniently store in a new list, called x_positions.
Next, we retrieve respondents' average partisanship as our node-level covariate of interest.

This is accomplished with the second call of ResIN_boots_extract(ResIN_executed,what="partisan_mean"). x_positions <-ResIN_boots_extract(ResIN_executed, what = "x") partisan_means <-ResIN_boots_extract(ResIN_executed, what = "partisan_mean") Since the objects extracted by ResIN_boots_extract() are stored as consecutively numbered lists, all we have to do is to generate a new list of the same length as our bootstrapped n = 1000 and subsequently fill the latter with the correlation estimates for each observed pair of partisan_means and x_positions. correlations <-list() for(i in 1:length(partisan_means)){ correlations[[i]] <-cor(partisan_means[[i]], x_positions[[i]])} correlations <-unlist(correlations) correlations <-as.data.frame(correlations) The final lines detail how we opted to quantify and visualize the resampled distribution.

text.text: ResIN() delivers several off-the-shelf estimates for node-level network statistics, including the strength, closeness, and betweenness-centrality, as well as expected node influence.
The raw metrics for each node-level statistic are stored in ResIN_out$ResIN_nodeframe.

The below code chunk shows how to visualize node-level differences in betweenness centrality; it is possible to set the argument plot_whichstat to either "Strength", "Closeness", "Betweenness", or "ExpectedInfluence".
These statistics are derived from internal function calls to qgraph:: centrality_auto and DirectedClustering::ClustF which were customized for ResIN graphs (Clemente, 2024; Epskamp et al., 2012).

text.text: The output in Figure 7 shows that the "strongly agree with the legality of gay marriage" response possesses the highest betweenness centrality within the broader, left-wing attitude cluster.
text.formatted: The output in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_8">7</ref> shows that the "strongly agree with the legality of gay marriage" response possesses the highest betweenness centrality within the broader, left-wing attitude cluster.

text.text: Descriptively, this indicates that the corresponding response node occupies a bridging position in the estimated layout, in the sense that a comparatively large share of the shortest paths linking the left and center-left clusters passes through it.
One possible reading is that this attitude is co-endorsed across otherwise distinct belief communities and therefore represents a point of overlap between them.

Betweenness centrality, however, is a descriptive property of the estimated co-endorsement structure rather than evidence about how attitudes are formed, communicated, or revised in cross-community dialogue.

Because the underlying data are crosssectional and aggregated across respondents, a bridging position of this kind cannot -in and of itself -establish that the issue in question is in fact more persuasive, less contentious, or more conducive to cross-cutting dialogue than attitudes occupying more peripheral positions in the network.
We suggest treating findings of this sort as hypothesis-generating rather than testing.
Descriptive network statistics can identify candidate attitudes whose cross-cluster standing may warrant closer examination with research designs capable of supporting confirmatory inference.

ResIN features two approaches to enhance network sparsity, i.e., the pruning of weak and (likely) idiosyncratic edges.
The first is based on raw p-value thresholds.
Users can specify remove_nonsignificant=TRUE which calls psych::corr.test() to perform pairwise t-tests on the individual correlation coefficients (Revelle, 2025).
text.formatted: Users can specify remove_nonsignificant=TRUE which calls psych::corr.test() to perform pairwise t-tests on the individual correlation coefficients <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Revelle, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If remove_nonsignificant=TRUE is set, ResIN() forces to zero all edge-weights whose p-values exceed the default threshold of p < 0.05; this threshold can be altered with the sign_threshold argument.
text.formatted: If remove_nonsignificant=TRUE is set, ResIN() forces to zero all edge-weights whose p-values exceed the default threshold of p < 0.05; this threshold can be altered with the sign_threshold argument.

text.text: The second approach implements false discovery rate (FDR) control via the Benjamini-Hochberg step-up procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).
text.formatted: The second approach implements false discovery rate (FDR) control via the Benjamini-Hochberg step-up procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Concretely, when remove_nonsignificant_ method="fdr", ResIN() first obtains edge-wise p-values (for the set of unique node pairs) and then applies a flexible adjustment across this family of tests (implemented via stats::p. adjust(method="BH")).
Edges are retained if their adjusted p-values fall below sign_threshold, which is interpreted as the target FDR level q; all remaining edges are pruned by setting their weights to zero.

Relative to a fixed per-edge threshold (e.g., p < 0.05), this approach adapts the rejection boundary to the global distribution of p-values and controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among retained edges, typically yielding greater power while maintaining a principled error rate (Benjamini & Yekutieli, 2001).
text.formatted: Relative to a fixed per-edge threshold (e.g., p < 0.05), this approach adapts the rejection boundary to the global distribution of p-values and controls the expected proportion of false discoveries among retained edges, typically yielding greater power while maintaining a principled error rate <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Benjamini & Yekutieli, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Pruning ResIN -networks can have benefits and drawbacks.

On the one hand, removing statistically insignificant edges can yield simpler structures which are easier to interpret and more likely to generalize to the target population of interest (Epskamp & Fried, 2018)

text.text: Such graphs co-locate people and their socially shared beliefs within the same network structure, treating the implicit connections explicitly, in the form of quasior para-social networks (Dinkelberg et al., 2021).

text.text: Multi-modal ResIN -networks thus enable community-detection and network centrality-based investigations at the level of individual survey takers, leading to more direct inferences about clustering and belief system centrality of individuals within a shared attitude space.

To generate such networks, users can simply set multimodal=T. By default, ResIN() determines the approximate location of each respondent within the basic, response-node graph, using the same force-directed method described above.
Crucially, the positions of the response nodes are held constant while respondent nodes freely circulate until a force equilibrium is found.

ResIN() outputs a 'node-frame' type data-frame, called coordinate_df which contains the x and y axis coordinates found for individual participants and a plot-able ggraph-object called multimodal_ggraph.
In the example in Figure 13, we further specified a cluster detection task to be performed on (both the regular ResIN and) the multimodal network variant.

text.text: ResIN() automatically calculates and returns the sum of participant and response nodes belonging to each of the obtained clusters.

Golino & Epskamp, 2017), and latent space item response models (LSIRM) embed respondents and items in a shared metric space in order to recover the dependence that a conventional measurement model leaves unexplained (Jeon et al., 2021; Kang & Jeon, 2024).

text.text: The latter thereby formally extend the latent space tradition in social network analysis (Hoff et al., 2002) to item response data. 10ResIN differs from all of these in three main respects.

text.text: As summarized in Table 1, ResINnodes represent individual item responses rather than items, ResIN -edges encode marginal (zero-order) co-endorsement rather than conditional dependence, and the method's primary inferential object is the geometry of the resulting layout rather than the structure implied by the adjacency matrix. 11 We consider each in turn and take up the practical limitations that follow from them in Section 5.
text.formatted: As summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>, ResINnodes represent individual item responses rather than items, ResIN -edges encode marginal (zero-order) co-endorsement rather than conditional dependence, and the method's primary inferential object is the geometry of the resulting layout rather than the structure implied by the adjacency matrix. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_5">11</ref> We consider each in turn and take up the practical limitations that follow from them in Section 5.

text.text: Perhaps the most consequential difference concerns the primary unit of analysis in each network method.

Because every response option enters the network as a dedicated node, ResIN models network structures that item-level methods cannot represent by construction: the two poles of a single item may occupy quite different positions within the latent space.

Similarly, 'neutral' or 'don't know' answers are not necessarily forced into the center (or periphery) of estimated attitude networks but may obtain unique, structurally and theoretically meaningful positions across the belief system space (see, e.g., Carpentras et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2025; Warncke et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Similarly, 'neutral' or 'don't know' answers are not necessarily forced into the center (or periphery) of estimated attitude networks but may obtain unique, structurally and theoretically meaningful positions across the belief system space (see, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Carpentras et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Warncke et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, by operationalizing nodes as item-responses, ResIN is capable of revealing potential asymmetries in the organization of belief-systems, thus making ResIN a particularly fruitful approach for investigating belief systems at the group level (e.g., as exemplified by Lüders et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, by operationalizing nodes as item-responses, ResIN is capable of revealing potential asymmetries in the organization of belief-systems, thus making ResIN a particularly fruitful approach for investigating belief systems at the group level (e.g., as exemplified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lüders et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: ResIN 's more fine-grained resolution also changes the meaning of node-level descriptive statistics.

Node strength in a GGM approximates the total unique association of a node within its local network environment, and thus its relative embeddedness or structural importancea property conceptually related to Converse's (1964) notion of static belief system centrality.
text.formatted: Node strength in a GGM approximates the total unique association of a node within its local network environment, and thus its relative embeddedness or structural importancea property conceptually related to <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Converse's (1964)</ref> notion of static belief system centrality.

text.text: Node strength in ResIN, by contrast, sums positive marginal correlations and therefore reflects the popularity of individual response options, a property closer to localized, opinion-based group prototypicality (Quayle, 2025).

The same holds for communities (Section 3.5).
EGA detects communities in a regularized partial-correlation network and interprets them as the dimensions underlying a set of items (H. F. Golino & Epskamp, 2017).
text.formatted: EGA detects communities in a regularized partial-correlation network and interprets them as the dimensions underlying a set of items (H. F. <ref type="bibr">Golino & Epskamp, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Communities in ResIN -graphs instead group mutually coendorsed response options, and can therefore distribute the response scale of a single item across two or more clusters.

That behavior is impossible by construction in item-level EGA, and is substantively informative in its own right, since it locates the point on a response continuum at which a position ceases to belong to one attitudinal camp and begins to belong to another.

Furthermore, because ResIN processes every data point at the nominal level of measurement, these communities of mutually endorsed responses can include non-numeric response options (e.g., "Don't know/prefer not to say") or even observational or behavioral metadata.
A second difference concerns the quantity that edges encode.

In a Gaussian graphical model, the Ising model, or a more general Markov random field, an edge represents a conditional association, i.e., the residual dependence remaining between two variables once every other variable in the system has been accounted for.
The absence of an edge is correspondingly informative, since it constitutes an explicit claim of conditional independence.
This property licenses reading such graphs as networks of direct interactions between attitude elements (Brandt & Sleegers, 2021; Dalege et al., 2016; Marsman et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This property licenses reading such graphs as networks of direct interactions between attitude elements <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brandt & Sleegers, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Dalege et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Marsman et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: ResIN -derived edges, by contrast, rest on unconditional, homophilic co-endorsement patterns (Carpentras et al., 2024; Quayle, 2025).
text.formatted: ResIN -derived edges, by contrast, rest on unconditional, homophilic co-endorsement patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carpentras et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Quayle, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: ResIN networks thus carry limited information about the extent to which co-endorsement is driven by direct rather than indirect influence between any given pair of attitudes.

Nevertheless, the statistical pipelines of other belief network methods can mask features exposed by ResIN, for example, attitude asymmetries between groups (e.g., Carpentras et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, the statistical pipelines of other belief network methods can mask features exposed by ResIN, for example, attitude asymmetries between groups (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Carpentras et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This contrast is especially instructive in the case of the CAN model, which shares with ResIN an interest in the spatial arrangement of attitudinal elements but differs in what nodes and edges are taken to represent.

Nodes in CAN-networks represent evaluative reactions toward a single attitude object, and CAN-edges are intended as direct causal connections within an individual's cognitive system, such that the estimated network is assumed isomorphic with the attitude construct itself (Dalege et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Nodes in CAN-networks represent evaluative reactions toward a single attitude object, and CAN-edges are intended as direct causal connections within an individual's cognitive system, such that the estimated network is assumed isomorphic with the attitude construct itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dalege et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: ResIN -nodes represent response options spanning distinct issue items, and ResIN -edges summarize population-level co-endorsement patterns.
A CAN-edge accordingly supports claims about how one evaluative reaction constrains another within a person, while a ResIN -edge captures which positions travel together across people (Quayle, 2025).
text.formatted: A CAN-edge accordingly supports claims about how one evaluative reaction constrains another within a person, while a ResIN -edge captures which positions travel together across people <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Quayle, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The third difference follows from the above.
Because individual edges carry little interpretive weight on their own, the object of inference shifts from the adjacency matrix to the layout it generates.
The collection of retained edges forms a global co-endorsement structure whose force equilibrium can reveal the major divisions between groups of respondents holding similar views.
ResIN -based analyses accordingly focus on the overall geometry rather than on individual links.

Spatial distances are a property of that layout rather than a directly estimated model parameter, which is what makes the bootstrapping routines of Section 3.3.3, rather than closedform standard errors, the appropriate instrument for quantifying uncertainty.

Among the methods considered here, latent space item response models bear the closest formal resemblance to ResIN, and that resemblance is closest of all to the multimodal extension introduced in Section 3.7.

Both approaches take item response data as input, embed the resulting entities in a shared low-dimensional metric space, interpret that space in terms of proximity, locate respondents alongside items or responses, and support clustering of the resulting configuration (Jeon et al., 2021; Kang & Jeon, 2024).
text.formatted: Both approaches take item response data as input, embed the resulting entities in a shared low-dimensional metric space, interpret that space in terms of proximity, locate respondents alongside items or responses, and support clustering of the resulting configuration <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Jeon et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kang & Jeon, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Conceptually, both also inherit the latent space tradition in social network analysis (Hoff et al., 2002), in which the probability of a tie declines in the distance between the positions of the two units involved.
text.formatted: Conceptually, both also inherit the latent space tradition in social network analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hoff et al., 2002)</ref>, in which the probability of a tie declines in the distance between the positions of the two units involved.

text.text: The substantive meaning of the latent network spaces produced by ResIN and LSIRM is nonetheless close to opposite.

The LSIRM augments a Rasch model with a distance term, such that the log odds of an affirmative response are a function of a person's ability θ p , an item's easiness b k , and a penalty -γd(ξ p , ζ k ).

In other words, the method renders a residual network space that represents the conditional dependence that remains once the main person and item effects have been accounted for (Jeon et al., 2021; Kang & Jeon, 2024).

In this last section, we summarize some principal limitations users should anticipate, along with our recommendations for working around them, and close with current efforts to address the most fundamental among them.
ResIN 's response-level resolution comes at the price of graph size and complexity.

Because the node set grows multiplicatively in the number of items, visual legibility and inferential precision can degrade well before they would for item-level alternatives, and researchers working with large item batteries should consider restricting the analysis to a theoretically motivated subset of items, pruning the network (Section 3.6), or collapsing response categories.

We should stress that the last of these entails a particularly substantive modeling decision: collapsing a seven-point scale to five or three points alters the node set, the cell frequencies underlying every correlation, and hence the estimated layout.
We recommend reporting the sensitivity of substantive conclusions to at least one alternative categorization.
ResIN also relies on adequate sample sizes and-more importantly-co-endorsement frequencies.

Each entry of Z (see Equation 4) is estimated from a 2 × 2 contingency table, so the binding constraint is typically not the overall sample size but the joint endorsement frequency of any given pair of response options. 13 Sparsely endorsed nodes may therefore enter Z with imprecisely estimated correlations and be positioned quite arbitrarily by the Fruchterman and Reingold, 1991 algorithm.

text.text: At the edge level, the principal simplification is the clipping of negative correlations (Equation 5).

Because the response options of a given item are mutually exclusive, the largest negative entries in Z are typically those between opposite poles of the same item, and these are already zeroed by the within-item restriction.
What clipping additionally removes are cross-item repul-sions, that is, pairs of positions endorsed together less frequently than chance would predict.

In structured attitude spaces this information is largely redundant, since the layout expresses repulsion through the constant repulsive force and the absence of attraction, and Carpentras et al., 2024 report no appreciable loss in the recovery of node positions.

That redundancy is not guaranteed to hold in every application, however, and the extent to which clipping alters the resulting geometry will depend on endorsement frequencies, response sparsity, and the dimensional structure of the data.
14   Two properties of the layout itself call for further attention.

First, the Fruchterman-Reingold algorithm is stochastic, and its solutions are identified only up to reflection along the dominant axis; we therefore highly recommend fixing an informative directional anchor node (Section 3.3.1).
Second, because spatial distances are not estimated parameters, they carry no analytic standard errors.
Bootstrapping (Section 3.3.3) provides the primary strategy for quantifying uncertainty around spatial quantities obtained with ResIN.
15   Another limitation stems from the fact that ResIN is not, as of this writing, derived from or based in a formal measurement theory.

Unlike the Ising model, which has been shown to stand in direct correspondence with multidimensional item response theory (Marsman et al., 2018), or the LSIRM discussed above, ResIN specifies no likelihood, no explicit data-generating process, and no formal criterion for model comparison.

We regard the integration of ResIN into such a framework, together with a systematic simulation study of the clipping, sparsity, and dimensionality questions raised above, as the most valuable directions for the further development of the method.
This paper provides an overview of ResIN for R. The package was designed with a 'one-stop shop' philosophy to facilitate end-to-end implementation of the ResIN method.
Beyond implementing the main computational algorithms, ResIN() produces various outputs that researchers are typically interested in.

These include co-variate statistics and individual-level position scores (Section 3.3.2), bootstrapped uncertainty bounds around these (Section 3.3.3), various network descriptive statistics (Section 3.4), and community detection (Section 3.5).

We also discussed more advanced methods and tools, such as network pruning (Section 3.6), generating multimodal structures (Section 3.7), and export to other statistical programming environments (Section 3.8).

While ResIN was first computationally introduced in the Python language (Carpentras et al., 2024), a comprehensive software suite centered around the method did not exist prior to the present implementation in R. 17 Researchers interested in making use of existing Python, C++, or Mathematica libraries for advanced network inference and visualization can, however, rely on the integrated igraph interface to import ResIN -graph objects generated in R into their desired language ecosystem, via the ResIN::as.igraph.ResIN() method.

text.text: Next, ResIN() derives the association structure among response nodes directly from the dummy response matrix using a unified correlation backend.
By default, the function obtains Pearson correlations (via stats::cor) from the dummy matrix, with optional support for both list-wise and pairwise handling of partial missingness.

When a survey-weight vector is provided with the weights argument (either as a dedicated object or via a column name indicating the weights variable within the supplied data-frame), ResIN() instead obtains weighted correlations.

In this case, the pair-specific effective sample size under unequal weights is obtained from Kish's design-effect formulation (Kish, 1965). 18 If users enable p-value-based network pruning (i.e., by setting remove_nonsignificant=TRUE), the function additionally produces uncertainty estimates for Pearson correlations to support edge filtering (either via raw p-values or Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery rate adjustment (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)).

In general, statistical quantities of interest generated with ResIN -graphs cannot rely on closedform probability distributions to derive uncertainty bounds.
Statistical inference therefore needs to rely on non-parametric bootstrapping procedures (Costantini et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Statistical inference therefore needs to rely on non-parametric bootstrapping procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Costantini et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Unfortunately, such procedures can be taxing -computationally and programming-wise -especially for users with limited statistical coding experience.

This is why ResIN provides a series of helper functions that were designed to simplify and accelerate the front-end programming, back-end computation, and downstream data extraction and visualization tasks associated with generating and evaluating statistical uncertainty.
More specifically, bootstrapping workflow with ResIN involves three steps, each of which is accomplished with a dedicated helper function: 1.
ResIN_boots_prepare() readies a given ResIN-class object for re-sampling tasks.
The additional parameters of this function, n and boots_type, determine the number of iterations and the basic kind of bootstrapping procedure users wish to perform.
Supported options for the latter argument are "resample" and "permute".
The former implements row-wise resampling of data rows with replacement and should be used to generate confidence intervals around particular point estimates.
This mode relies on the sample_n function provided by dplyr (Wickham et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This mode relies on the sample_n function provided by dplyr <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Wickham et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The boots_type="permute" option prescribes a permutation test by distorting all the entries in the original data-matrix, X (which is implemented with a nested for loop which simultaneously "re-organizes" both data rows and columns via the base::sample() function).
This procedure derives zerocentered, null-hypothesis distributions around parameters of interest.

In both cases, the resample_size argument determines sample size within each bootstrap iteration which can be useful in statistical power-and sensitivity analyses. 19 Survey weights can be supplied as a numeric weights vector of the same length as the original dataset, using the weights argument.

A few sensible guardrails hard-coded in ResIN_boots_prepare() prevent the automatic console transfer of n re-estimated network plots during the bootstrapping procedure.
ResIN_boots_execute() takes the output generated by ResIN_boots_prepare() and implements the pre-defined bootstrapping procedure.
If the parallel option is set to TRUE, the function exploits CPU parallelism via the doSNOW engine (Daniel et al., 2022).

If detect_cores is set to TRUE, all available CPU cores detected by parallel::detectCores() will be employed; this number can also be offset with the core_offset argument which reduces the number of workers by the supplied integer value.
Essentially, ResIN_boots_execute() calls n instances of the ResIN() function, each supplied with the instructions generated by ResIN_boots_prepare().

Once the re-estimation procedure has concluded, ResIN_boots_extract() provides a search-and-grab utility to locate and summarize the output list generated by ResIN_ boots_execute() for particular quantities of interest.
Users solely need to specify a search term with the what argument, e.g., what="x" for bootstrapped node positions along the dominant ResIN axis.

text.text: ResIN not only shares much of its conceptual and operational scope with a rapidly expanding family of BNMs, but also possesses a number of stand-alone qualities that users should weigh when choosing among available approaches.

This section attempts to briefly situate the method (as implemented in package version 2.3.1) relative to other popular BNMs with available software implementations in R. While a systematic methods comparison lies well beyond the scope of a package tutorial, our aim here is to provide basic guidance on whether ResIN is an appropriate instrument for a given research task.

text.text: The multimodal ResIN extension (Section 3.7) is the closest point of contact between the approaches, since it likewise places respondents and response nodes within a single spatial representation.

text.text: Both treat a two-mode structure-units on one side, items or positions on the other-and interpret proximity as a higher propensity for the corresponding tie.
The main difference lies in what the coordinates represent.

In the Hoff et al., 2002 latent network space approach, latent positions are parameters of a probability model for tie formation, jointly estimated for all units and reported with posterior uncertainty.

In multimodal ResIN, by contrast, endorsement ties are observed rather than modeled, and respondent coordinates are obtained by holding the response-node layout fixed and relaxing respondents to a force equilibrium within it.

Respondent positions therefore inherit the attitude geometry rather than co-determine it, which keeps estimation fast and the resulting scores directly interpretable, but forfeits the model-based uncertainty that the latent space tradition supplies.

text.text: Unlike any established BNM, ResIN can treat every type of response as nominal and can hence include nonnumeric response options such as refusal ("Don't know/prefer not to say", "Question not asked"), open-ended responses, and various types of discrete metadata as dedicated nodes within the estimated network.

text.text: First, the LSIRM is estimated by MCMC, which delivers posterior uncertainty for every position and a spike-and-slab test of whether a latent space is warranted at all, at the computational cost of Bayesian estimation; ResIN imposes none of these requirements and typically returns a solution in seconds, but forgoes closed-form, model-based inference.
Second, the LSIRM operates on items, with dichotomous responses in its base specification and extensions to two-parameter and continuous responses
